prime.problem: An LFU cache must evict the key used least often, breaking ties by least recently used, in O(1). Scanning all keys on eviction is O(n); a heap of (count, time) is O(log n) and fills with stale entries because every touch changes a key's priority.
prime.fits: The first Coding and design card. It is the linked-bucket-list idea (one bucket per count, counts move by 1) with an OrderedDict per bucket for the recency tie-break, and a single min integer instead of a linked list of buckets.
expect: keys: count → OrderedDict of keys, oldest first
min: the smallest count in use
why min only resets to 1 or steps up by 1
prime.goal: Implement get and put in O(1), trace an eviction with a tie, and explain why exact LFU is rarely what production caches use.

attend: Why does every get or put on a key move it from bucket c to the end of bucket c + 1?
Why can min only reset to 1 or step up by exactly 1?
Within the min bucket, why is the oldest key at the front?
What does the source's key_count.remove(key) bug break, if the outputs stay correct?
Why does a newly inserted key become the next victim the moment it arrives?

must: Each touch raises a key's count by exactly 1 → it moves from bucket c to bucket c + 1 → appending puts it at the newest end → each bucket is in recency order for free → the LRU tie-break is popitem(last=False)

min tracks the lowest non-empty bucket → a new key enters at count 1, so min = 1 after insert → otherwise min changes only when its bucket empties during a touch, and then the key went to min + 1 → no search for the minimum, ever
Evict = keys[min].popitem(last=False), then delete from val and cnt → all steps are dict or OrderedDict operations → O(1) average per get and put

Exact counts never decay → yesterday's hot keys squat with big counts while newcomers enter at 1 and are evicted first → production caches approximate LFU with decaying or sampled counters (Redis allkeys-lfu, TinyLFU)
elevated: Update an existing key before checking capacity → otherwise updating at capacity evicts a different key first (the bug the testing card hunts down)
reference: Redis Morris counters and TinyLFU's sketch

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the three maps and min just before put(4, 4) in the card's trace, then explain in 3–4 sentences why eviction is O(1) and how ties are broken.
checklist: the victim is the front of keys[min]: 1, used longer ago than 3
each touch moves a key one bucket up, to the newest end
min resets to 1 on insert, steps up by 1 when its bucket empties

retrieve.q: Explain why this cache never needs to search for the minimum count.
answer: counts change only by +1 per touch, and new keys enter at 1
so the minimum either becomes 1 (insert) or moves up by 1 (its bucket emptied because its last key moved up)
a single integer tracks it exactly

retrieve.q: Walk through op 6, get(3), in the card's trace (buckets 1: [3], 2: [1], min 1).
answer: 3 moves from bucket 1 to the end of bucket 2: 2: [1, 3]
bucket 1 is now empty and was min, so it is deleted and min = 2
next eviction will take 1, the older key in bucket 2

retrieve.q: A product team asks for LFU because popular items should stay cached. What goes wrong with exact LFU when popularity shifts, and what would you propose?
answer: old counts never decay, so formerly hot keys hold their slots
every newcomer enters at count 1 and is evicted first, so new hot keys struggle to stay
use decaying or approximate counts (Redis allkeys-lfu, TinyLFU admission), or plain LRU if recency predicts reuse

compare.q: LFU and All O(1) both keep a bucket per count. Why does LFU get away with a dict of buckets and one integer, while All O(1) needs a linked list of buckets?
answer: LFU only asks for the minimum, and counts only go up
so min can be maintained by resets to 1 and +1 steps
All O(1) needs both min and max, and counts go down too
a linked list keeps the whole order so both ends are O(1)

compare.q: An interview LFU vs a production cache: what does each optimise, and which assumptions of this card break at scale?
answer: the interview version: exact least-frequent eviction in O(1)
production: hit rate under shifting traffic with bounded memory per key
exact counts don't decay; production uses decay, sampling and admission filters
in a shared cache, concurrency and memory overhead per key matter too

predict.q: Capacity 2: put(1), put(2), get(2), get(2), put(3), get(1), get(3), put(4). Before tracing: which key does put(4) evict under LFU, and which would plain LRU evict at the same point?
predict.answer: LFU evicts 3: at put(4) the counts are 2 → 3 and 3 → 2, so the minimum bucket holds only 3. LRU would evict 2, whose last use (op 4) is older than 3's (op 7). This is where the two policies diverge; on the card's own trace they happened to agree.
